kernelIdea: "p and q" is true only when both are; "p or q" is true when at least one is (inclusive or). A statement always false is a contradiction; always true, a tautology.

kernels.l1: AND means both of them. OR means at least one of them — and both still counts.
kernels.l2: A telling with AND in it is true only when both parts are true. A telling with OR in it is true when at least one part is true, and both parts being true is still fine.
kernels.l3: Joining two statements with and gives a statement that is true only when both are true. Joining them with or gives one that is true when at least one is true — including when both are. A statement that is always false is a contradiction; one that is always true is a tautology.
kernels.l4: "p and q" is true exactly when both are true. "p or q" is true when at least one is — including when both are. A statement false in every row of its truth table is a contradiction; one true in every row is a tautology.
kernels.l5: *And* is true only on the row where both parts are true; *or* is false only on the row where both fail. Always-false statements are contradictions, always-true ones tautologies.
kernels.l6: *And* is true only when both parts are; *or* is true whenever at least one is, so both counts too. A statement false in every row is a contradiction; true in every row, a tautology — and the second is the license for splitting a proof into cases.
kernels.l7: Conjunction is true only when both conjuncts are; disjunction is inclusive, false only when both disjuncts fail. A contradiction is a statement false under every assignment; a tautology, one true under every assignment.
kernels.l8: ∧ and ∨ are the meet and join of the two-element Boolean algebra; contradictions and tautologies are its bottom and top elements, and they anticipate ∩ and ∪ on sets.
